The "Magnificent Seven" is a grouping of stocks used to describe some of the largest companies in the world that have helped lead the U.S. stock market higher over the past decade. It is made up of:

Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL)

Nvidia

Microsoft

Alphabet

Amazon

Meta Platforms

Tesla

For U.S.-listed stocks, all seven of these are in the top 10, so being on this list is a big deal. However, 2026 hasn't been the greatest year for the Magnificent Seven. The S&P 500 is up about 12.3% this year, and only three stocks are outperforming it: Apple, Amazon, and Microsoft. But which one of these is doing the best? It's the non-AI one.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
Apple leads all Magnificent Seven stocks

The top performer so far in 2026 has been Apple, up about 29%. That's practically double the second-best performer, Amazon, which has risen around 15%. So, what has separated Apple from the competition? I think there are two reasons.

First, Apple really isn't an AI stock. While its products have some AI features, it's not spending hundreds of billions of dollars on data centers like every other company on this list (besides Nvidia, which is selling the equipment for these data centers). As a whole, the market has been a bit bearish on the AI buildout lately, and Apple has been a haven for investors who aren't as keen on the long-term prospects of AI.

In fact, Apple is the only stock among the top 10 largest companies on U.S. exchanges that doesn't have significant AI investments or business cases riding on the AI buildout. This has made it a safe haven for non-AI investors and has boosted its stock.

Another reason Apple has done well this year is that its iPhone 17 lineup was the most popular of any of its previous models. This has driven sales growth and has made Apple a respectable business again.

However, Apple's day of reckoning could be coming. Outside of Tesla (which has a sky-high valuation of 424 times trailing earnings), Apple is by far the most expensive stock in the Magnificent Seven.

NVDA PE Ratio data by YCharts

As a result, I think the stock could be getting a bit too pricey, and investors need to watch out. Apple's strong performance this year hasn't come entirely from business results, and if the market flips its stance on AI and becomes bullish on it again, Apple's stock could sell off in favor of some AI-focused investments. It's about as good as it gets for Apple sentiment right now. As a result, I don't think Apple stock is a buy right now.

Commodity prices have fluctuated wildly over the past several years. Gold prices reached a record high of nearly $5,600 per ounce in January, but they have since plunged 26%. But it may not be over for the precious metal as fiscal deficits rise and geopolitical tensions persist.

According to the World Gold Council, central banks, including those in Asia, Eastern Europe, and the Middle East, have been accumulating gold and diversifying reserves. Central bank gold purchases have doubled since 2022, following the freeze of approximately $300 billion in Russian foreign exchange reserves.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

In the third quarter, central banks purchased 321 metric tons of gold to their reserves, the fastest pace of buying since late 2024. According to research from JPMorgan Chase, gold prices could climb to $6,300 per ounce by 2027.

Image source: Getty Images.

While gold is rising amid rising debts and debasement fears, copper is rising amid strong demand from infrastructure projects, including data centers, power grid upgrades, and renewable energy build-outs. Analysts forecast multi-year copper supply deficits, and the World Bank recently forecast copper prices to rise another 18% in 2027.

Commodities have come into focus in recent years amid growing government deficits and robust infrastructure demand, and these three stocks let investors capture the upside and high margins as demand booms and supply remains tight.

Freeport-McMoRan is a massive producer of copper

Freeport-McMoRan (NYSE: FCX) is one of the world's largest copper producers and also produces large amounts of gold and molybdenum. It owns a range of Tier-1 assets across North America, South America, and Indonesia, and its business spans large-scale open-pit and underground mining, as well as downstream smelting, refining, and rod production.

In the mining industry, building a new mine from scratch (greenfield projects) is a massive undertaking that can take decades before delivering production. What makes Freeport stand out among competitors is its slew of brownfield projects, which expand or modify existing mines. Management points out that almost all of Freeport's growth pipeline is brownfield, which lowers capital intensity and enables new production in a few years.

Through the first three quarters of this year, Freeport has sold almost 2.1 billion pounds of copper, with projected full-year sales of 3 billion pounds. In addition, Freeport produced 234,000 ounces of gold and sold 105,000 ounces during the third quarter, realizing $4,273 per ounce.

Altria Group (NYSE: MO), parent company of Marlboro maker Philip Morris USA, has one of the highest forward yields among stocks in the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC). It has also raised its quarterly dividend annually for 57 consecutive years, placing it among the Dividend Kings, stocks with at least 50 years of consecutive dividend growth.

While this company's days of high growth are behind it, a path remains for the stock to sustain and keep on slightly growing its quarterly payouts in the years ahead. Dividend investors should still consider it a buy.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
What a $10,000 investment in Altria can generate in annual dividend income

With Altria trading for around $78 per share, a $10,000 investment in the stock equates to around a 128-share position. Altria pays a $1.11-per-share quarterly dividend. Annualized, that comes out to $4.44 per share. Multiply that by 128 shares, and you get $568.32 in annual dividend income, giving it a 5.7% annual dividend yield. That's over 5 times the annual dividend yield of the S&P 500, which currently stands at around 1.1%.

Altria most recently declared a dividend increase in August, raising the quarterly payout by 4.7%. This is in line with management's current dividend growth policy, which targets "mid-single-digit dividend per share growth annually."

Why Altria stands to sustain its dividend stalwart status

Yes, Altria's 88.5% payout ratio looks very high. However, with rising cigarette prices and growing sales of "smokeless" products, the company's dividend policy appears sustainable.

Altria recently raised its full-year earnings growth guidance to between 4.5% and 6%, bolstering confidence that the company can both maintain its dividend and keep raising it at a modest pace in the years ahead.

"Going smokeless" remains a greater challenge for Altria than the success competitors like Philip Morris International have had in this area, but as sales of its smokeless products continue to help augment overall growth, the stock appears well positioned to maintain its status as both a high-yield dividend stock and a Dividend King.

Limping toward the end of 2026, Centrus Energy (NYSE:LEU) stock fell 18.6% in September and continued to decline last month. Analysts took a more bearish stance on the nuclear stock, and investors were clearly paying attention.

According to data provided by S&P Global Market Intelligence, Centrus Energy stock fell 26% in October, while the S&P 500 dipped 0.5%.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

Firms are skeptical of the company's acquisition of a key supplier

On Oct. 19, Centrus announced its acquisition of Westerman Holdings, which the company characterizes as one of its largest and most diversified suppliers. Centrus believes that the transaction, funded with about $95 million in cash and $21 million in equity, will contribute to its adjusted earnings per share in the first year following its closing.

Centrus lauded the acquisition as "a significant milestone ... as it builds supply chain resilience while diversifying its revenue base." Westerman provides Centrus to a variety of industries beyond nuclear, including oil and gas and other industrial sectors.

Investors immediately expressed their disapproval of the acquisition. Centrus shares dropped more than 4% on Oct. 19 from the stock's previous close.

On Oct. 20, analysts began to weigh in on the acquisition -- and the opinions were hardly encouraging. Roth Capital slashed its price target on Centrus to $115 from $188, maintaining a neutral rating. According to Thefly.com, the firm updated its model after Centrus acquired Westerman Holdings and believes that the company's third-quarter financial results could disappoint investors.

In the ensuing days, firms shared a variety of other downwardly revised price targets.

On Oct. 20, Barclays lowered its price target to $150 from $207.

On Oct. 23, UBS dropped its price target to $120 from $185.

On Oct. 26, JPMorgan reduced its price target to $120 from $180.

Centrus is a leading provider of nuclear fuel and services for the nuclear power industry. One area in which the company distinguishes itself is the production of high-assay low-enriched uranium (HALEU), a specialized form of nuclear fuel required by small modular reactors (SMRs), the next generation of nuclear reactors. At the end of September 2026, Centrus reported a backlog of $5.4 billion for both low-enriched uranium (LEU) and HALEU businesses.

Shares of AppLovin (NASDAQ: APP) spent much of this year in the doghouse as investors worried about rival Unity Software's (NYSE: U) progress. AppLovin missed second-quarter expectations after its model performance failed to improve at its usual pace. However, the stock surged after its third-quarter results zoomed past expectations.

Given the adtech company's growth and valuation, AppLovin still looks like a buy after this rebound. Let's dig into its results and prospects to see why the artificial intelligence (AI) stock still looks like a good buy.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

AppLovin's strong growth continues

AppLovin has been one of the biggest beneficiaries of using AI to drive growth in its core business, with the launch of its AI adtech platform, Axon 2.0, in 2023 being a game changer for the company.

Image source: The Motley Fool.

This was on full display once again in the third quarter as revenue soared 55% to $2.18 billion. That topped the $2.07 billion analyst consensus, as compiled by Bloomberg.

The growth was driven by both improvements in its core gaming business and its start to gain momentum in the consumer industry. Its gaming business grew nearly 50%, fueled by the partial rollout of the transition to a new model.

It said the current model transition that it is undergoing is as meaningful as the launch of its AXON 2 platform and that it enhances performance in areas where there isn't as much data, such as with newer advertisers, smaller advertisers, and in newer categories like the consumer space. It said advertiser performance was strong in the quarter, with customers seeing higher profitability on their ad spending, leading to an increase in ad budgets.

Meanwhile, CEO Adam Foroughi said that any success competitors were seeing was not impacting its growth. He said that this is not a zero-sum game and that their improvements benefit the market as a whole.

AppLovin's newer consumer vertical saw revenue grow by triple digits year over year in the quarter. This business continues to add runway, and the company believes this vertical will help the overall company compound at 30% annually over the long term.

Adjusted earnings per share (EPS) also came in above expectations. EPS from continuing operations climbed 76% from $2.39 a year ago to $4.30, topping the consensus by $0.26. Adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) climbed 59% year over year to $1.84 billion.

Investing to profit from the AI build-out can be difficult. There are so many options, ranging from computing companies to application plays to energy companies. All of these are bound to benefit in one way, but choosing the best isn't easy. However, I think there's one company that may cut through all of that noise and provide a top investment opportunity: Taiwan Semiconductor (NYSE: TSM).

It looks like a practically guaranteed winner in the AI build-out, and it's easy to see why.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
Taiwan Semiconductor has a grip on the chip industry

Taiwan Semiconductor is a logic chip fabrication company: Simply put, it manufactures the chips designed by its clients, most of which lack any foundries of their own. All of the major AI computing unit manufacturers -- Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA), AMD (NASDAQ: AMD), and Broadcom (NASDAQ: AVGO), and others -- utilize TSMC's services.

They have to, as no other chip foundry has the capacity to serve as a viable alternative. During Q2, TSMC's massive manufacturing infrastructure allowed it to take in 72.5% of chip foundry revenue in the world. That capacity dominance makes it difficult for any other company to rise and steal its leading clients away.

However, even if it were more of an option, TSMC's clients don't have many reasons to want to switch foundry partners, either. TSMC has best-in-class technology and a reputation for fantastic production yields. That makes it a great company to partner with. There's a reason why TSMC has grown to become the giant that it is.

As for the AI build-out, as long as companies continue to need more and more computing capacity, TSMC will see large orders for chips. It has projected that from 2024 to 2029, revenues from its AI chip business will grow at a compound annual rate in the mid-to-high 50% range, and during the company's Q3 conference call, CEO C.C. Wei said that its growth rate "probably will be higher."

That will benefit shareholders immensely.

Lastly, the stock isn't priced outrageously.

TSM PE Ratio (Forward) data by YCharts.

At 23 times forward expected earnings, Taiwan Semiconductor is trading at a discount relative to its typical level at this time of year. So, not only is it a great long-term investment in the AI build-out, but it's also a timely buy. Opportunities like this don't often appear, and investors should take advantage of the stock while it's a bit cheaper than historical levels. While TSMC may not provide the best long-term AI returns, I am confident that it is practically guaranteed to do well.

title: A Stock Market Crash Could Be Life-Changing for Investors Who Have These 3 Things
detail:
A Stock Market Crash Could Be Life-Changing for Investors Who Have These 3 Things
Lawrence Nga, The Motley Fool
Sun, November 8, 2026 at 12:35 PM CST 5 min read
NVDA
Trade NVIDIA on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

A stock market crash can be frightening. Portfolio values plunge, economic forecasts worsen, and investors begin to question whether they should sell before things get worse. But for prepared investors, a crash can also create opportunities to build substantial wealth. Some of the world's best businesses can suddenly become available at prices that seemed impossible just months earlier.

The challenge is knowing what to buy and having the patience and financial resources to act.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Three things can make a significant difference:

The right time horizon.

A shopping list of great businesses.

Capital set aside to take advantage of opportunities.

Image source: Getty Images.
The right time horizon

The first requirement is a long investment horizon. If you need your money next year for a house deposit or other major expense, a market crash can be disastrous. You might be forced to sell investments at depressed prices.

But if you are investing money you won't need for the next 10 years, or longer, you have more flexibility to withstand temporary declines and allow businesses to compound their earnings.

Consider a company whose share price falls 40% during a market panic, even though its competitive position and long-term earnings prospects remain intact. An investor with a long time horizon can potentially benefit from the lower price. Someone who needs the money immediately may have no choice but to sell.

The key is to invest with money you can afford to leave untouched, rather than money you might need in the near future.

A shopping list of great businesses

Imagine your favorite supermarket announcing a 30% discount. You would probably know which products you want before walking through the doors.

Investing should work the same way. Rather than scrambling to find stocks during a market crash, prepare a list of businesses you would love to own at the right price.

For example, Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOGL) (NASDAQ: GOOG) is an interesting company to watch. It owns Google Search, YouTube, and Google Cloud, while investing heavily in artificial intelligence (AI). These businesses give it several ways to benefit from the growing use of AI.

Another example is Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN). Its e-commerce operations, cloud computing business, and advertising division provide multiple sources of growth. AWS also gives Amazon exposure to rising demand for AI computing.

title: Why Nvidia Stock Looks Like a Bargain Right Now
detail:
Why Nvidia Stock Looks Like a Bargain Right Now
Patrick Sanders, The Motley Fool
Sun, November 8, 2026 at 11:10 AM CST 4 min read
NVDA
Trade NVIDIA on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) has made investors a tremendous amount of money over the past several years. But lately, the artificial intelligence chipmaker has been heading in the wrong direction.

Shares have been essentially flat so far in 2026 and have fallen about 22% from their all-time high. That's quite a reversal for a company whose revenue more than doubled in its most recent quarter.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

And I think investors are getting an opportunity with Nvidia stock.

Image source: Getty Images.

Nvidia reports its fiscal third-quarter earnings on Nov. 17, and I'm expecting another blowout performance. The company's financial results and the extraordinary demand for AI computing suggest its growth story has plenty of room to run.

Nvidia's business isn't slowing down

In its fiscal second quarter, which ended July 26, Nvidia generated $96.2 billion in revenue, up 106% from a year earlier. Data center revenue reached $89 billion, an increase of 117%.

Those are remarkable growth rates for a company operating at Nvidia's scale.

Management expects third-quarter revenue of approximately $108 billion, representing another 12% sequential increase at the midpoint. Nvidia also forecasts a non-GAAP gross margin of 74%, suggesting it expects to maintain substantial pricing power despite its enormous sales volume.

And there are good reasons to believe demand remains strong. SK Hynix, a major supplier of high bandwidth memory used in AI accelerators, has indicated that its advanced memory capacity is effectively sold out for years. That matters, because Nvidia's GPUs need that memory to handle increasingly demanding AI workloads.

Meanwhile, Nvidia's Vera Rubin platform is already in full production, with systems being deployed by major cloud providers and AI infrastructure companies.

Customers aren't waiting for AI computing demand to disappear. They're spending billions to secure more capacity.

The sell-off creates an opportunity

The latest weakness in Nvidia stock reflects concerns about the enormous cost of AI infrastructure and the possibility that political opposition could slow data center construction.

Those aren't imaginary risks. If companies struggle to obtain electricity or construction permits, some GPU deployments could be delayed.

But there's a difference between a delay in building data centers and a collapse in demand for AI computing. Nvidia has already demonstrated that it can sell enormous quantities of increasingly sophisticated chips while maintaining exceptional margins. Its next earnings report will provide another opportunity to see whether that demand is holding up.

title: The 1 Stock I'd Buy With $2,500 in November and Not Check Until 2051
detail:
The 1 Stock I'd Buy With $2,500 in November and Not Check Until 2051
Micah Zimmerman, The Motley Fool
Sun, November 8, 2026 at 11:50 AM CST 5 min read
NVDA
Trade NVIDIA on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Even when you have high-conviction ideas, buying a stock and not looking at it for 25 years is a tall order. There are a couple of ways to approach the problem. You can pick a business whose model is built to last, one that works in good economies and bad. Or you can pick a company with a track record of adapting that has already survived a few of the things that kill retailers. Or you can look for the rare company that is both.

The one I would pick is a company that sells last season's designer handbags next to a $7 scented candle, and has been doing some version of that since 1976.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
TJX works in booms and in busts

TJX Companies (NYSE: TJX) runs T.J. Maxx, Marshalls, HomeGoods, and a handful of other banners across over 5,200 stores in ten countries. The model is simple to describe and nearly impossible to copy: buy brand-name merchandise that full-price retailers overordered, undersold, or canceled, and sell it at 20% to 60% below their prices in a store that changes every week. The customer never knows what she will find, which is why she keeps coming back.

What makes it a 25-year stock to me is that the model has no bad weather. When the economy is strong, brands overproduce and TJX has more to buy. When the economy weakens, shoppers trade down and TJX has more people to sell to. Its sales held up through the 2008 recession and grew during the inflation-driven stretch that followed, and management has said in its annual reports that it has been gaining market share.

In its most recent quarter, with consumers under pressure and tariffs scrambling the supply chain, comparable sales rose 4%, and CEO Ernie Herrman said the availability of branded merchandise "continues to be outstanding." Other retailers' problems are TJX's inventory.

A company that keeps adapting

The second test is adaptability, and TJX passes it in a way that is easy to miss because the company never announces a reinvention. It simply adds. HomeGoods did not exist until 1992; it now does $10 billion a year and grew comparable sales 7% last quarter.

TK Maxx in Europe and Winners in Canada were small experiments that are now two of the fastest-growing parts of the company, up 7% and 6%. Sierra, a tiny outdoor chain, is opening stores. Management said in August that it now sees room for 7,500 stores worldwide under its existing banners, up 500 from its prior target, and will speed up openings to 4% a year starting in 2027.
